# Preliminaries

# Problem 1

The p-value for a two-sided T test of the hypotheses $H_0: \mu = 15$ versus $H_A: \mu \neq 15$ is 0.03.

(a) Does the 99% T confidence interval for $\mu$ using this same sample include 15? Why or why not?

(b) Does the 95% T confidence interval for $\mu$ using this same sample include 15? Why or why not?


# Problem 2

The file `parental_leave.csv` contains information on crowdsourced parental leave data (in weeks) for 1601 different companies.  

```{r}
leave <- read_csv("../data/parental_leave.csv")

# Remove spaces from column names
names(leave) <- make.names(names(leave))

# Tidy numeric columns
leave <- leave %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Paid.Maternity.Leave, Unpaid.Maternity.Leave,
                 Paid.Paternity.Leave, Unpaid.Paternity.Leave),
            as.numeric) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0)
```

(a) Mutate a column for total paid leave by adding the weeks of paid maternity and paternity leave. Optionally, give the columns shorter names that are easier to reference.

(b) Filter the data to only include the "Educational Services: College & Universities" industry.  Create a histogram of total paid leave and comment on its shape.

(c) Comment on why a T test for the mean might still be an appropriate method, even though the total paid leave data does not look normal.


(d) Build a 98% T CI for the average total weeks of paid leave of companies in "Educational Services: College & Universities", and interpret the results. You must do this by hand, but you can check your results with `t.test()`.

(e) Calculate the point estimate and standard error from the data.  Find a T critical value with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom based on $\alpha = 0.02$ and use this to construct the CI.


# Problem 3

Perform a test at the 2% level to determine whether the "Educational Services: College & Universities" average total paid leave is greater than 10 weeks.  State hypotheses, report a test statistic and p-value. You must do this by hand, but you can check your results with `t.test()`.


# Problem 4

Re-calculate the p-value from problem 3, but use a standard normal distribution instead of a $T_{n-1}$ distribution.  Why are the results very similar?



# Problem 5

Continue working with the parental leave data.

```{r}
leave <- read_csv("../../data/parental_leave.csv")

# Remove spaces from column names
names(leave) <- make.names(names(leave))

# Tidy numeric columns
leave <- leave %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Paid.Maternity.Leave, Unpaid.Maternity.Leave,
                 Paid.Paternity.Leave, Unpaid.Paternity.Leave),
            as.numeric) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0)
```

(a) Re-do the basic data tidying from homework 9 problem 5(a): Mutate a column for total paid leave by adding the weeks of paid maternity and paternity leave. Optionally, give the columns shorter names that are easier to reference.

(b) Consider comparing companies in "Educational Services: College & Universities" (ESCU) to companies in "Healthcare: Hospitals & Clinics" (HHC).  Create and print a table summarizing the mean, standard deviation, and sample size for both groups.

(c) Assess the equal variances assumption for these two groups of data by comparing the ratio of standard deviations.  Even if the standard deviations are similar "enough", why might we want to not assume equal variances?


# Problem 6

Assuming unequal variances, build a 95% CI for the difference in average total weeks of paid leave between the ESCU and HHC industries and interpret the results. You must do this by hand, but you can check your results with `t.test()`.


# Problem 7

Does the educational industry give more paid leave than the healthcare industry?  Perform a hypothesis test of 
$$H_0: \mu_{ESCU} - \mu_{HHC} = 0 \quad \text{versus}\quad H_A: \mu_{ESCU} - \mu_{HHC} > 0$$
with $\alpha = 0.05$, assuming unequal variances.  You must do this by hand, but you can check your results with `t.test()`.


# Problem 8

Repeat the by-hand test in problem 4, but instead write hypotheses for $\mu_{HHC} - \mu_{ESCU}$ (the order of subtraction is switched).  Show that you get identical results to problem 4.
